S049-01.notes: The colon clause (lists costs and benefits but takes no position) defines noncommittal. Partisan and inflammatory contradict the neutral, detailed report. Redundant has no support in the text.

S049-02.notes: The text sets up a puzzle and then gives the explanation found by analyzing samples. B goes too far (no recommendation is made), C brings in later empires, and D mentions mining, which the text never discusses. Factual check: this matches Jackson et al. (2017). Seawater moving through the concrete reacted with volcanic ash and grew aluminous tobermorite and phillipsite crystals in pores and cracks. Later lime-clast self-healing work (2023) is a separate finding and does not contradict this text.

S049-03.notes: Only D isolates learning by watching other crows: these birds were never captured and hatched later, yet they still scold the mask. A supports learning from the crows' own experience, not observation. B and C do not address how crows learn. Factual check: this matches Marzluff's University of Washington mask study, where the scolding spread to uncaptured crows and to later generations.

S049-04.notes: The limitation is sampling: only birds within about 50 m of the trails could be detected, so the data say nothing about species away from the trails. A and D draw the causal or preference conclusions the caution is meant to warn against. C is unsupported. A strong student might ask whether 'away from the trails' fits the trailhead-versus-interior comparison, but B is still clearly the best answer.

S049-05.notes: Text 2 makes a self-selection or generalizability objection, which C paraphrases. A reverses his view. B contradicts the data, which he does not dispute. D introduces worker preference, which neither text mentions.

flags.note: Possible cue: A is the only choice that gives computed counts and also repeats the 'even though a smaller percentage' clause from the claim. Test-takers can match it to the claim without doing the arithmetic. Typical SAT quantitative items carry similar cues, though.

S049-06.notes: Arithmetic: 0.20 x 800 = 160 and 0.30 x 200 = 60, so A is accurate. B supports only the percentage half of the claim. C gives sample sizes but no count of people who said yes. D is irrelevant to the comparison.

S049-07.notes: With either/or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'her two coauthors', so it must be plural. A, C and D are all singular. C also clashes in tense with 'next month's'. Only B works when inserted.

S049-08.notes: The opening participial phrase must modify the person who spent the decade: the historian. A and C make 'conclusion' the subject, and B makes 'it' the subject, so all three dangle. Inserting D gives 'letters, the historian concluded that they were written...', which is grammatical and correctly punctuated.

S049-09.notes: The second sentence gives a specific detail for the general claim of 'far heavier traffic'. Nevertheless and Instead signal contrast, and Likewise signals a parallel point, so none of them fits.

flags.note: In D, 'carry more water than any other rivers' is slightly loose: the two rivers rank first and second, so each one outflows every other river. The intended reading is clear and accurate, and D is the only choice that states a similarity.

S049-10.notes: A, B and C each describe a difference or a fact about one river only. Facts check out: the Amazon has the largest discharge and the Congo the second largest; both drain tropical rainforests; the Amazon is about 6,400 km long and the Congo about 4,700 km; and the Congo reaches more than 200 m deep (about 220 m).
